simple: deciding the command in advance and never checking what really happened.
analogy: Wei pushing the pedals "the usual way" whatever the wind does.
precise: control in which the command is computed from the setpoint (and perhaps a model) only; the measured output does not influence the command.

simple: measuring what happens and using it to choose the next command, again and again.
analogy: Nia watching her speedometer and pushing harder or softer.
precise: control in which a measurement of the output is fed back and compared with the setpoint, and the difference (the error) drives the command; also called feedback control.

simple: the part of the program that decides the command.
analogy: the rider's brain.
precise: the rule, usually code run at a fixed rate, that maps the setpoint and (in closed loop) the measurement to an actuator command. Not the same as a hardware controller chip or a Kubernetes controller.

simple: the thing being controlled.
analogy: the pipes and the water heater.
precise: the part of a control system whose output is to be regulated, including the actuator when it is not modelled separately; written G(s) or P(s).
source: B1 of F0-70 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: anything from outside that pushes the output away from where you want it.
analogy: the wind, or a flat tyre.
precise: an input to the plant that the controller does not choose, such as a load torque or a change in supply voltage; good control keeps its effect on the output small.

simple: a rule, written as maths or code, that predicts what the plant will do.
analogy: knowing "if I push like this, I go about this fast".
precise: an equation (here a step-by-step update) relating the plant's inputs to its output; never exact, and the gap between model and plant is called model mismatch.

simple: how much output you finally get per unit of steady input.
analogy: how many degrees hotter per unit of heater setting, once everything has settled.
precise: K = lim y(t)/U for a step of size U in a stable system; for a motor's speed, rad/s per volt.
source: B1 of F0-68 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the "speed setting" of an RC circuit: bigger means slower.
analogy: how long the tank takes to fill most of the way. [proposed mapping, awaiting registration in guide 8.1; see HW101 NOTES.md]
precise: τ = R × C, in seconds when R is in ohms and C in farads; after one τ a charging capacitor has covered 1 − e−1 ≈ 63.2 % of the way to the supply voltage.
source: D2 of F1-05 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics"); R1 of F1-05 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the time between two runs of the controller.
analogy: how often Nia glances at the speedometer.
precise: the fixed interval T at which a digital controller reads its sensor and updates its command (the command is held constant in between); here T = 10 ms. MA301 calls the same interval the sample time Δt.

simple: the further you are from the goal, the harder you correct.
analogy: "a little slow, a little push; very slow, a big push".
precise: the control law u = Kp·e with e = r − y; the P of PID. RB101 called it proportional correction.

simple: the number that says how hard to correct for each unit of error.
analogy: how much harder Tomás pushes for each km/h he is slow.
precise: the constant Kp in u = Kp·e, with units of command per unit of error (here volts per rad/s).

simple: the difference between setpoint and output that is left once everything has settled.
analogy: the shower ending up a little cooler than wanted, because Mira only turns the tap in proportion to how cold she feels.
precise: e(∞) = limt→∞(r − y); for a step r and a stable loop, e(∞) = r/(1 + L(0)) when H = 1 (final value theorem, F0-69).
source: D1 of F0-70 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); R2 of F0-70 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how strongly the whole loop reacts, going once round it.
analogy: how much speed Tomás gains, in the end, for each km/h he notices he is slow.
precise: the product of the gains round the loop at steady state, here L = Kp·Kdc (dimensionless); MA301 writes it L(0).

simple: the actuator cannot deliver more than its limit, however hard the controller asks.
analogy: the tap turned hard against its stop.
precise: a nonlinearity u = clamp(v, umin, umax) between controller and plant; while it is active, the loop is effectively open and the linear transfer-function analysis does not apply.
source: B1 of F0-70 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); R3 of F0-70 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how far the output goes past its final value, as a percentage.
analogy: how far past the true weight the needle swings first.
precise: Mp = (ymax − y∞)/y∞; for the standard second-order system Mp = exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)).
source: B1 of F0-68 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); R2 of F0-68 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the number that multiplies "how far from settled" every control period.
analogy: how much of his speed error Tomás still has at each glance at the speedometer, and whether it has flipped from too slow to too fast.
precise: for a first-order sampled loop y[k+1] − y∞ = p·(y[k] − y∞); |p| < 1 is stable, p < 0 alternates in sign. MA302 (F0-79) treats poles in the z-plane in general.

simple: a part of the command that grows for as long as there is an error, and stays when the error is gone.
analogy: Tomás's extra push that builds up while he is slow.
precise: the term Ki·S of the controller output, where S is the integral of the error over time; in discrete form S[k] = S[k−1] + e[k]·T. The I of PID.

simple: how fast the extra push grows for each unit of error.
analogy: how quickly Tomás's patience runs out.
precise: the constant Ki multiplying the integral of the error; units of command per (error × time), here V per (rad/s · s) = V per rad. Some texts write Ki = Kp/Ti with an integral time Ti.

simple: a total to which you add "value × Δt" at every sample.
analogy: Kofi's list of flow readings added up.
precise: S[k] = S[k−1] + x[k]·Δt, the rectangle rule of F0-65 updated one sample at a time.
source: D1 of F0-66 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a controller that adds "how far off now" and "how long and how far off".
analogy: Tomás's two habits together.
precise: u = Kp·e + Ki·∫e dt, clamped to the actuator's range; a PID controller with Kd = 0.

simple: the integral keeps growing while the actuator is already at its limit, and later causes a big overshoot.
analogy: Tomás's "more, more" on the hill that makes him shoot past his speed at the top.
precise: the accumulation of the integral state while the actuator is saturated, so that the controller's output stays saturated after the error changes sign, until the excess integral has been removed by error of the opposite sign.

simple: any trick that stops the integral from growing while the actuator is at its limit.
analogy: Tomás telling himself "I am already pushing as hard as I can, stop asking for more".
precise: a modification of the integral update during saturation, for example conditional integration (freeze it) or back-calculation (bleed it towards the value the limit allows); implemented in F9-21.

simple: a part of the command that reacts to how fast things are changing.
analogy: Amara braking early because she is approaching the line fast.
precise: the term Kd·de/dt of the controller output; in discrete form Kd·(e[k] − e[k−1])/T, or −Kd·(y[k] − y[k−1])/T when taken from the measurement. The D of PID.

simple: how strongly to react to each unit of "how fast".
analogy: how firmly Amara brakes for each bit of extra speed.
precise: the constant Kd; units of command per (error unit per second), here N per (m/s) = N·s/m.

simple: anything that slows a moving thing in proportion to its speed, so swings die out.
analogy: the shock absorber on a bicycle fork.
precise: a force or effect opposing velocity, −c·v; it removes energy from an oscillation. MA301 (F0-68) measures it with the damping ratio ζ.

simple: a single number saying how strongly the swinging is slowed down.
analogy: how sticky the scale's mechanism is: a little, and it wobbles a lot; a lot, and it creeps to the value.
precise: ζ = c/(2√(k·m)) for a mass–spring–damper; under-damped 0 < ζ < 1 (overshoots), critically damped ζ = 1, over-damped ζ > 1.
source: B1 of F0-68 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how long until the output stays close to its final value for good.
analogy: how long before you can read the scale.
precise: the last time the response is outside a band (here ±2 %) around y∞; the estimate 4/(ζωn) holds for moderately under-damped systems only.
source: B1 of F0-68 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); R2 of F0-68 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a huge one-sample spike in the command when the setpoint jumps.
analogy: slamming the brakes because the chalk line was suddenly redrawn somewhere else.
precise: the impulse Kd·Δr/T produced by differentiating the error when the setpoint r changes by Δr in one sample.

simple: taking the "how fast" from the measured output instead of from the error.
analogy: watching how fast the bicycle moves, not how fast the line moves.
precise: D = −Kd·dy/dt; equal to Kd·de/dt whenever the setpoint is constant, and free of derivative kick.

simple: small wobbles in readings become big wobbles in the speed you compute from them.
analogy: a one-centimetre wobble over two seconds looks like a fast fill.
precise: a sample error of size ε produces an error up to 2ε/Δt in a two-point difference; the shorter Δt, the larger.
source: D1 of F0-66 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); R2 of F0-66 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: choosing the controller's gains so the system behaves the way you want.
analogy: Keanu adjusting his bicycle between practice rides.
precise: selecting Kp, Ki, Kd (and filter and limit settings) so that the closed loop meets a stated specification, by experiment, by rule or by optimisation.

simple: a written list of measurable things the controlled system must do.
analogy: the coach's card.
precise: requirements such as maximum overshoot, maximum settling time, maximum steady-state error and maximum actuator effort for a defined test (here a 1 m step), each with a number and a pass/fail rule.

simple: how long the output takes to get most of the way to the new target.
analogy: the time from leaving the start line to nearly reaching the top of the ramp.
precise: here the time from 10 % to 90 % of the step; other definitions exist, so a specification must state which one it uses.

simple: one number that adds up how wrong the output was, and for how long.
analogy: the total distance-times-seconds Keanu spent away from the line.
precise: IAE = ∫|e(t)| dt, computed here as the sum of |e[k]|·T; units m·s. Smaller is better; a common cost for comparing tunings.

simple: trying every combination of gains on a grid and keeping the ones that pass.
analogy: riding the practice ramp with every saddle height and every gear, and keeping the setups that meet the card.
precise: an exhaustive search over a finite set of gain vectors, each evaluated by simulation against the specification and ranked by a cost such as IAE.

simple: a rule that computes a command from the error now, the sum of past errors, and how fast the error changes.
analogy: adjusting the tap from how far the bath is from full, how long it has been short, and how fast it is filling.
precise: u[k] = Kp·e[k] + Ki·S[k] + Kd·D[k], with S a running sum and D a (filtered) difference of the error or of the measurement (RB202 F9-21).
source: B1 of F0-66 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: stop adding to the integral while the output is stuck at its limit and the error would push it further.
analogy: not building up more "I've been off for ages" while already steering as hard as possible.
precise: an anti-windup method: the integral update is skipped when the unclamped output is beyond a limit and the error has the sign that drives it further beyond.

simple: smoothing applied to the rate of change before D uses it.
analogy: judging speed from the last few lamp posts, not from one twitch of the head.
precise: here a first-order low-pass rf += α(r − rf) with α = T/(τ + T); τ = 0 means no filter.

simple: changing settings or modes without a jump in the output.
analogy: changing gear without a jolt.
precise: a property of a controller implementation: switching gains, or switching from manual to automatic, leaves u[k] continuous. Storing the integral in output units makes gain changes bumpless.

simple: checking every number before the controller uses it.
analogy: ignoring a lane marking that is clearly a leaf.
precise: refusing non-finite setpoints and measurements (NaN, ±∞, MA302) and invalid configurations, so that one bad value cannot poison the stored state.

simple: A small check of one function, with an input and the answer you expect.
analogy: Tasting one sauce on its own.
precise: Code that calls a unit (here: one function) with chosen inputs and compares the results with expected values computed independently.
source: D3 of F2-08, R1 of F2-08 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1)

simple: a short list of functions through which the control program talks to the hardware, and nothing else.
analogy: the handlebars, pedals and brakes: the rider never touches the chain directly.
precise: an abstract class (here MotorIo: read the encoder counter, set the duty cycle) with one implementation per back end, such as a simulator or a particular kit.

simple: working out a machine's numbers by testing it, not by reading them off a label.
analogy: finding out how a new bicycle accelerates by pedalling it once with a fixed effort.
precise: estimating the parameters of a model (here the static gain and time constant of a first-order model) from measured input and output data.

simple: a range of small commands that produce no motion at all.
analogy: pushing the pedal so gently that the bicycle does not move.
precise: a dead zone in an actuator's input–output curve, often caused by static friction; here an exercise value of 0.5 V below which the simulated motor does not turn.

simple: a gentle check, before closing the loop, that "forward" on the motor really reads as "forward" on the sensor.
analogy: rolling the bicycle a little to check the speedometer counts up, not down.
precise: a short open-loop drive with a small positive command, accepted only if the measured speed is clearly positive; a sign error would turn negative feedback into positive feedback.

simple: a check that stops the motor when it is being pushed hard but is not moving.
analogy: stopping pedalling when the wheel is stuck in a drain grate.
precise: software that sets the output to zero when the command magnitude stays above a threshold while the measured speed stays near zero for longer than a set time (here duty above 0.5 and speed below 5 rad/s for 0.3 s).

simple: testing a machine fixed in place on a table, with protection, before letting it do real work.
analogy: checking the brakes while standing still.
precise: a supervised test with the mechanism clamped, the load removed or controlled, limits set low and an emergency stop within reach.

simple: the differences between how something behaves in the simulator and on the real machine.
analogy: the street being bumpier than the playground.
precise: the effect of everything the model leaves out or gets wrong (friction, deadband, noise, delays, supply sag, wiring); BR-08 treats it in depth.
